claim: In human tuberculosis (TB), necrotic granulomas and cavities are the most prominent and treatment recalcitrant lesion types.
source: In human tuberculosis (TB), necrotic granulomas and cavities are the most prominent and treatment recalcitrant lesion types (Canetti, 1955).
evidence: Supported by citation to Canetti, 1955

claim: The major histopathological features of necrotic granulomas and cavities are a caseous or necrotic core surrounded by a cuff of immune cells including lymphocytes, epithelioid macrophages, foam cells or lipid-laden macrophages, and interspersed neutrophils and epithelial cells.
source: The major histopathological features of these lesions are a caseous or necrotic core surrounded by a cuff of immune cells including lymphocytes, epithelioid macrophages, foam cells or lipid-laden macrophages, and interspersed neutrophils and epithelial cells (Leong et al., 2011; Dannenberg, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leong et al., 2011 and Dannenberg, 2006

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is found intracellularly in macrophages and foamy macrophages in TB lesions.
source: In these lesions, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiologic agent of TB, is found intracellularly in macrophages and foamy macrophages (Peyron et al., 2008), neutrophils (Dallenga and Schaible, 2016; Berry et al., 2010), epithelial cells (Scordo et al., 2016) and dendritic cells (Tailleux et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peyron et al., 2008

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is found intracellularly in neutrophils in TB lesions.
source: In these lesions, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiologic agent of TB, is found intracellularly in macrophages and foamy macrophages (Peyron et al., 2008), neutrophils (Dallenga and Schaible, 2016; Berry et al., 2010), epithelial cells (Scordo et al., 2016) and dendritic cells (Tailleux et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dallenga and Schaible, 2016 and Berry et al., 2010

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is found intracellularly in epithelial cells in TB lesions.
source: In these lesions, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiologic agent of TB, is found intracellularly in macrophages and foamy macrophages (Peyron et al., 2008), neutrophils (Dallenga and Schaible, 2016; Berry et al., 2010), epithelial cells (Scordo et al., 2016) and dendritic cells (Tailleux et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scordo et al., 2016

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is found intracellularly in dendritic cells in TB lesions.
source: In these lesions, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiologic agent of TB, is found intracellularly in macrophages and foamy macrophages (Peyron et al., 2008), neutrophils (Dallenga and Schaible, 2016; Berry et al., 2010), epithelial cells (Scordo et al., 2016) and dendritic cells (Tailleux et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tailleux et al., 2003

claim: Mtb can establish a durable infection in foamy macrophages leading to replication and/or long term survival in a dormant state.
source: Mtb can establish a durable infection in foamy macrophages leading to replication and/or long term survival in a dormant state (Peyron et al., 2008; Russell, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peyron et al., 2008 and Russell, 2007

claim: TB granulomas present with increasingly abnormal vasculature from the periphery inward.
source: TB granulomas present with increasingly abnormal vasculature from the periphery inward (Datta et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Datta et al., 2015

claim: Most vessels are compressed along the lesion periphery and collapsed within the interior of the cellular rim in TB granulomas.
source: Most vessels are compressed along the lesion periphery and collapsed within the interior of the cellular rim.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: Vascular dysfunction in TB granulomas leads to impaired vascular function and a gradual decrease of small molecule penetration as the distance from the granuloma outer edge increases.
source: This leads to impaired vascular function and a gradual decrease of small molecule penetration as the distance from the granuloma outer edge increases (Datta et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Datta et al., 2015

claim: Vascular dysfunction culminates in a complete lack of blood vessels in the necrotic core of TB granulomas.
source: Vascular dysfunction culminates in a complete lack of blood vessels in the necrotic core.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: Mtb-infected foam cells or foamy macrophages largely concentrate along the interface between the cellular and caseous regions of the lesion.
source: Mtb-infected foam cells or foamy macrophages largely concentrate along the interface between the cellular and caseous regions of the lesion (Peyron et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peyron et al., 2008

claim: Reaching adequate drug concentrations at the sites of infection is critical in achieving sterilization and clinical utility in TB disease.
source: Efficacy and drug distribution studies in animal models of TB disease have shown that reaching adequate drug concentrations at the sites of infection is critical in achieving sterilization and clinical utility (Irwin et al., 2014; Irwin et al., 2016; Prideaux et al., 2015a; Tanner et al., 2018; Zimmerman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Irwin et al., 2014; Irwin et al., 2016; Prideaux et al., 2015a; Tanner et al., 2018; Zimmerman et al., 2017

claim: Most TB drugs exhibit differential partitioning between the cellular and necrotic regions of pulmonary lesions.
source: Using analytical approaches and MALDI mass spectrometry imaging (MSI), we previously showed that most TB drugs exhibit differential partitioning between the cellular and necrotic regions of pulmonary lesions (Irwin et al., 2016; Prideaux et al., 2015a; Zimmerman et al., 2017; Prideaux et al., 2011; Prideaux et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Irwin et al., 2016; Prideaux et al., 2015a; Zimmerman et al., 2017; Prideaux et al., 2011; Prideaux et al., 2015b

claim: In MDR-TB patients, treatment success is associated with the use of fluoroquinolones.
source: In MDR-TB patients, treatment success is associated with the use of FQs (Ahuja et al., 2012) and, not surprisingly, it follows that FQ resistance is associated with poor clinical outcome (Bastos et al., 2014; Falzon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ahuja et al., 2012

claim: FQ resistance is associated with poor clinical outcome in MDR-TB patients.
source: In MDR-TB patients, treatment success is associated with the use of FQs (Ahuja et al., 2012) and, not surprisingly, it follows that FQ resistance is associated with poor clinical outcome (Bastos et al., 2014; Falzon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bastos et al., 2014 and Falzon et al., 2013

claim: Moxifloxacin, levofloxacin and gatifloxacin are used to treat MDR-TB.
source: Moxifloxacin (MXF), levofloxacin (LVX) and gatifloxacin (GTX), three later generation FQs, are used to treat MDR-TB, although GTX production for systemic administration was recently terminated due to its side effect profile.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: GTX production for systemic administration was recently terminated due to its side effect profile.
source: Moxifloxacin (MXF), levofloxacin (LVX) and gatifloxacin (GTX), three later generation FQs, are used to treat MDR-TB, although GTX production for systemic administration was recently terminated due to its side effect profile.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: MXF is included in many 'universal' regimens under clinical evaluation to treat both drug susceptible and MDR-TB.
source: In addition, MXF is included in many 'universal' regimens under clinical evaluation to treat both drug susceptible and MDR-TB ((Gillespie, 2016; Diacon et al., 2012); http://www.endtb.org/clinical-trial; ClinicalTrials.gov), and thus has the potential to become a pivotal TB drug.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gillespie, 2016; Diacon et al., 2012 and references to clinical trials

claim: MXF kills non-replicating Mtb persisters in ex vivo caseum at concentrations that are achieved clinically in caseous foci.
source: We have recently shown that MXF kills non-replicating Mtb persisters in ex vivo caseum (Sarathy et al., 2018) at concentrations that are achieved clinically in caseous foci (Prideaux et al., 2015a; Heinrichs et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sarathy et al., 2018; Prideaux et al., 2015a; Heinrichs et al., 2018

claim: MXF, LVX and GTX each formed a narrow rim of high signal intensity directly adjacent to the caseous center of the granuloma in MALDI MSI ion maps.
source: In two-dimensional MALDI MSI ion maps, MXF, LVX and GTX each formed a narrow rim of high signal intensity directly adjacent to the caseous center of the granuloma, as well as additional rings or pockets of higher intensity further outward from the necrotic center (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: Observation from MALDI MSI data shown in Figure 1

claim: MXF, LVX and GTX formed additional rings or pockets of higher intensity further outward from the necrotic center in MALDI MSI ion maps.
source: In two-dimensional MALDI MSI ion maps, MXF, LVX and GTX each formed a narrow rim of high signal intensity directly adjacent to the caseous center of the granuloma, as well as additional rings or pockets of higher intensity further outward from the necrotic center (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: Observation from MALDI MSI data shown in Figure 1

claim: There is approximately 1.5 to 2-fold higher signal of fluoroquinolones in cellular lesions than in uninvolved lung and caseum.
source: We found approximately 1.5 to 2-fold higher signal in cellular lesions than in uninvolved lung and caseum for all three FQs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of MALDI MSI data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: MXF and GTX concentrations were higher in cellular areas than in caseum and uninvolved lung, although only marginally so.
source: Overall, MXF and GTX concentrations were higher in cellular areas than in caseum and uninvolved lung, although only marginally so.
evidence: Observation from laser capture microdissection coupled with mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: LVX exhibited irregular patterns of distribution between the cellular and caseous regions.
source: LVX exhibited irregular patterns of distribution between the cellular and caseous regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Observation from laser capture microdissection coupled with mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: High resolution H and E images of mature necrotic granulomas reveal concentric layers including a ring of foamy macrophages with high lipid droplet contents directly subtending the caseous core, a layer mostly composed of lymphocytes, and a thick layer rich in clusters of less foamy macrophages in a background of lymphocytes.
source: To understand the drivers of heterogeneous FQ distribution in cellular granuloma regions, we generated high resolution H and E images of mature necrotic granulomas (Figure 2A–F), revealing the following concentric layers from the caseum outward: a ring of foamy macrophages with high lipid droplet contents directly subtending the caseous core, a layer mostly composed of lymphocytes, and a thick layer rich in clusters of less foamy macrophages in a background of lymphocytes (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Observation from H&E histology shown in Figure 2

claim: Small clusters or ribbons of epithelial or stromal cells as well as interspersed neutrophils were found in most layers of mature necrotic granulomas.
source: Small clusters or ribbons of epithelial or stromal cells as well as interspersed neutrophils and were found in most layers (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Observation from H&E histology shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: Mtb bacilli were mostly found in foamy macrophages and in association with karyorrhectic neutrophils in the caseous foci of necrotic granulomas and cavities.
source: Mtb bacilli were mostly found in foamy macrophages and in association with karyorrhectic neutrophils (dying cells containing mostly fragmented chromatin irregularly distributed throughout the cytoplasm) in the caseous foci of necrotic granulomas and cavities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Observation from histology shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H

claim: Average MXF contents were significantly different across the majority of ROIs.
source: We found that average MXF contents were significantly different across the majority of ROIs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) with a between-ROI variability of 43.4%.
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A

claim: There is a between-ROI variability of 43.4% in MXF contents.
source: We found that average MXF contents were significantly different across the majority of ROIs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) with a between-ROI variability of 43.4%.
evidence: Statistical analysis of MALDI MSI data

claim: There is a positive association between MXF abundance and the fraction of macrophages.
source: Using Spearman rank correlation, we found a positive association between MXF abundance and the fraction of macrophages, and an inverse correlation with the relative distance from lesion border and the necrosis fraction (Figure 3—source data 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Spearman rank correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: There is an inverse correlation between MXF abundance and the relative distance from lesion border.
source: Using Spearman rank correlation, we found a positive association between MXF abundance and the fraction of macrophages, and an inverse correlation with the relative distance from lesion border and the necrosis fraction (Figure 3—source data 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Spearman rank correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: There is an inverse correlation between MXF abundance and the necrosis fraction.
source: Using Spearman rank correlation, we found a positive association between MXF abundance and the fraction of macrophages, and an inverse correlation with the relative distance from lesion border and the necrosis fraction (Figure 3—source data 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Spearman rank correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B

claim: There was no significant association between MXF intensity signal and the percentage of other immune cell types in ROIs.
source: There was no significant association between MXF intensity signal and the percentage of other immune cell types in ROIs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Spearman rank correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C

claim: Accounting for histiocyte fraction reduced the between-ROI MXF variability from 44.0% to 28.3%.
source: Using nonlinear mixed effect modeling (nonMEM) with the full dataset, we found that accounting for histiocyte fraction reduced the between-ROI MXF variability from 44.0% to 28.3%, which further decreased to 20.0% when relative distance of ROI to lesion edge was integrated in the model.
evidence: Nonlinear mixed effect modeling analysis

claim: Integrating relative distance of ROI to lesion edge in the model decreased the between-ROI MXF variability to 20.0%.
source: Using nonlinear mixed effect modeling (nonMEM) with the full dataset, we found that accounting for histiocyte fraction reduced the between-ROI MXF variability from 44.0% to 28.3%, which further decreased to 20.0% when relative distance of ROI to lesion edge was integrated in the model.
evidence: Nonlinear mixed effect modeling analysis

claim: Factoring the fraction of the ROI occupied by necrotic tissue reduced the between-ROI MXF variability from 20.0% to 18.9%.
source: Factoring the fraction of the ROI occupied by necrotic tissue further reduced the variability from 20.0% to 18.9% (Table 1), significantly improving the correlation.
evidence: Nonlinear mixed effect modeling analysis shown in Table 1

claim: Integrating the fraction of other immune cell types further decreased the residual unexplained variability but not significantly so.
source: Integrating the fraction of other immune cell types further decreased the residual unexplained variability but not significantly so (Table 1).
evidence: Nonlinear mixed effect modeling analysis shown in Table 1

claim: Immune cells other than macrophages do not significantly influence the partitioning of MXF.
source: This suggested that immune cells other than macrophages do not significantly influence the partitioning of MXF.
evidence: Inference from nonlinear mixed effect modeling analysis

claim: The model could predict ROI-specific MXF abundance using histiocyte fraction, relative distance from lesion margin and necrosis content.
source: We found that the model could predict ROI-specific MXF abundance using histiocyte fraction, relative distance from lesion margin and necrosis content (Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4D,E).
evidence: Model validation shown in Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4D,E

claim: MXF, LVX and GTX all accumulated in macrophages at higher levels than in lymphocytes, neutrophils and epithelial cells in vitro.
source: Drug uptake in each cell type revealed that MXF, LVX and GTX all accumulated in macrophages at higher levels than in lymphocytes, neutrophils and epithelial cells in vitro (Figure 5A).
evidence: In vitro drug uptake assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: More than 80% of the macrophages appeared Nile Red positive after infection with γ-irradiated M. tuberculosis.
source: Foamy macrophages were derived from differentiated primary macrophages via infection with γ-irradiated M. tuberculosis, upon which more than 80% of the macrophages appeared Nile Red positive, that is with a high lipid droplet content.
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Less than 30% of the non-stimulated macrophages were Nile Red positive.
source: In contrast, less than 30% on the non-stimulated macrophages were Nile Red positive (Figure 5B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Fluoroquinolone uptake was significantly higher in foamy than in non-foamy macrophages.
source: Fluoroquinolone uptake was significantly higher in foamy than in non-foamy macrophages (Figure 5C).
evidence: In vitro drug uptake assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The mean ratio of macrophage versus foamy macrophage uptake for fluoroquinolones is around 2.
source: Given the high inter-donor variability in absolute uptake, we also plotted the macrophage versus foamy macrophage uptake ratio for each individual donor, showing a mean ratio around 2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Analysis of in vitro drug uptake data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: FQ uptake is higher in foamy macrophages, where Mtb bacilli largely reside in vivo, than in regular macrophages in vitro.
source: Thus FQ uptake is higher in foamy macrophages, where Mtb bacilli largely reside in vivo, than in regular macrophages in vitro.
evidence: Conclusion from in vitro drug uptake assay data

claim: FQs are actively transported in and out of eukaryotic cells.
source: This may be due to differential regulation of transporters and efflux pumps since FQs are actively transported in and out of eukaryotic cells (Maeda et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2018; Mulgaonkar et al., 2013; Rudin et al., 1992; Michot et al., 2005), and foamy macrophages are known to differentially express selected transporters such as ABCG1 and ABCA1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) compared to non-foamy phagocytes (Lorkowski et al., 2001; Canfrán-Duque et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maeda et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2018; Mulgaonkar et al., 2013; Rudin et al., 1992; Michot et al., 2005

claim: Foamy macrophages are known to differentially express selected transporters such as ABCG1 and ABCA1 compared to non-foamy phagocytes.
source: This may be due to differential regulation of transporters and efflux pumps since FQs are actively transported in and out of eukaryotic cells (Maeda et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2018; Mulgaonkar et al., 2013; Rudin et al., 1992; Michot et al., 2005), and foamy macrophages are known to differentially express selected transporters such as ABCG1 and ABCA1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) compared to non-foamy phagocytes (Lorkowski et al., 2001; Canfrán-Duque et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lorkowski et al., 2001 and Canfrán-Duque et al., 2017

claim: Processes such as pinocytosis have been implicated in foam cell biogenesis and could be upregulated in these cells.
source: Alternatively, processes such as pinocytosis have been implicated in foam cell biogenesis and could be upregulated in these cells (Michael et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Michael et al., 2013

claim: Drug tolerant M. tuberculosis persisters are present in the foam cells of human lung lesions.
source: Regardless of the underlying mechanism, the finding that FQs are preferentially taken up by all phagocytes has positive clinical implications since drug tolerant M. tuberculosis persisters are present in the foam cells of human lung lesions (Peyron et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peyron et al., 2008

claim: M. tuberculosis bacilli are found in viable and necrotic neutrophils, which constitute a privileged site of bacterial replication.
source: On the other hand, M. tuberculosis bacilli are also found in viable and necrotic neutrophils, which constitute a privileged site of bacterial replication (Mishra et al., 2017; Kimmey et al., 2015; Diedrich et al., 2016) and where MXF uptake was significantly lower than in macrophages.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mishra et al., 2017; Kimmey et al., 2015; Diedrich et al., 2016

claim: MXF uptake was significantly lower in neutrophils than in macrophages.
source: On the other hand, M. tuberculosis bacilli are also found in viable and necrotic neutrophils, which constitute a privileged site of bacterial replication (Mishra et al., 2017; Kimmey et al., 2015; Diedrich et al., 2016) and where MXF uptake was significantly lower than in macrophages.
evidence: Inference from in vitro drug uptake data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The distribution of fluoroquinolones within the cellular cuff of mature TB lesions is uneven.
source: Here we have combined high resolution MALDI MSI, qualification of cell types in H and E stained sections, quantitative image analysis and nonlinear modeling to show that (i) the distribution of FQs within the cellular cuff of mature TB lesions is uneven and (ii) the heterogeneous distribution of MXF in TB lesions is driven by the macrophage content, the distance from lesion border and the extent of necrosis.
evidence: Summary of findings from MALDI MSI and modeling

claim: The heterogeneous distribution of MXF in TB lesions is driven by the macrophage content, the distance from lesion border and the extent of necrosis.
source: Here we have combined high resolution MALDI MSI, qualification of cell types in H and E stained sections, quantitative image analysis and nonlinear modeling to show that (i) the distribution of FQs within the cellular cuff of mature TB lesions is uneven and (ii) the heterogeneous distribution of MXF in TB lesions is driven by the macrophage content, the distance from lesion border and the extent of necrosis.
evidence: Summary of findings from MALDI MSI and modeling

claim: FQs are preferentially taken up by macrophages relative to other immune cell types typically found in TB lesions.
source: In vitro uptake assays in human blood cells were developed to confirm that the FQs are preferentially taken up by macrophages relative to other immune cell types typically found in TB lesions, and even more strongly so in foamy macrophages where Mtb establishes long term infection and dormancy.
evidence: Summary of in vitro drug uptake findings

claim: FQs are even more strongly taken up by foamy macrophages where Mtb establishes long term infection and dormancy.
source: In vitro uptake assays in human blood cells were developed to confirm that the FQs are preferentially taken up by macrophages relative to other immune cell types typically found in TB lesions, and even more strongly so in foamy macrophages where Mtb establishes long term infection and dormancy.
evidence: Summary of in vitro drug uptake findings

claim: The results are consistent with published data on the accumulation of FQs in macrophage cell lines.
source: Our results are consistent with published data on the accumulation of FQs in macrophage cell lines (Carlier et al., 1990; Michot et al., 2006), constitute an advance over assays relying on immortal cell lines in which expression of transporters and efflux pumps can be significantly altered, and demonstrate that uptake is significantly lower in human neutrophils and lymphocytes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Carlier et al., 1990 and Michot et al., 2006

claim: Uptake of FQs is significantly lower in human neutrophils and lymphocytes compared to macrophages.
source: Our results are consistent with published data on the accumulation of FQs in macrophage cell lines (Carlier et al., 1990; Michot et al., 2006), constitute an advance over assays relying on immortal cell lines in which expression of transporters and efflux pumps can be significantly altered, and demonstrate that uptake is significantly lower in human neutrophils and lymphocytes.
evidence: In vitro drug uptake data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The clear correlation between MXF abundance and relative distance from the outer lesion border is in keeping with previous studies showing that functionally abnormal vasculature increases as the distance from granuloma border increases, leading to correspondingly impaired small molecule distribution.
source: The clear correlation between MXF abundance and relative distance from the outer lesion border is in keeping with previous studies showing that functionally abnormal vasculature increases as the distance from granuloma border increases, leading to correspondingly impaired small molecule distribution (Datta et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Datta et al., 2015

claim: Therapies thought to achieve vessel normalization appear to improve small molecule delivery to TB lesions.
source: In these studies, the authors showed that therapies thought to achieve vessel normalization, and thus improve vascular function, appear to improve small molecule delivery to TB lesions (Datta et al., 2015) or potentiate TB therapy (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Datta et al., 2015 and Xu et al., 2018

claim: Therapies thought to achieve vessel normalization appear to potentiate TB therapy.
source: In these studies, the authors showed that therapies thought to achieve vessel normalization, and thus improve vascular function, appear to improve small molecule delivery to TB lesions (Datta et al., 2015) or potentiate TB therapy (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2018

claim: In oncology, excessive angiogenesis generates a disorganized and leaky blood vessel network leading to poor drug delivery to the tumor core.
source: These observations are reminiscent of oncology drug penetration concepts, where excessive angiogenesis generates a disorganized and leaky blood vessel network leading to poor drug delivery to the tumor core (Azzi et al., 2013; Di Paolo and Bocci, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Azzi et al., 2013 and Di Paolo and Bocci, 2007

claim: Foamy macrophages are known to differentially express selected transporters such as ABCG1 and ABCA1 compared to non-foamy phagocytes.
source: This may be due to differential regulation of transporters and efflux pumps since FQs are actively transported in and out of eukaryotic cells (Maeda et al., 2007; Weiner et al., 2018; Mulgaonkar et al., 2013; Rudin et al., 1992; Michot et al., 2005), and foamy macrophages are known to differentially express selected transporters such as ABCG1 and ABCA1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) compared to non-foamy phagocytes (Lorkowski et al., 2001; Canfrán-Duque et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lorkowski et al., 2001 and Canfrán-Duque et al., 2017

claim: The methodology is broadly applicable to the high-resolution mapping of any drug in diseased tissue, particularly when multiple cell types are present in complex lesions, tumors, atherosclerotic plaques.
source: The methodology is broadly applicable to the high-resolution mapping of any drug in diseased tissue, particularly when multiple cell types are present in complex lesions, tumors, atherosclerotic plaques, to name a few.
evidence: Statement about the applicability of the methodology

claim: The co-localization of drugs and immune cell populations supported by in vitro uptake data is a powerful new tool to guide in silico modeling and simulations of drug distribution in TB lesions or any complex structure where drug penetration is paramount.
source: The co-localization of drugs and immune cell populations supported by in vitro uptake data is a powerful new tool to guide in silico modeling and simulations of drug distribution in TB lesions (Pienaar et al., 2017) or any complex structure where drug penetration is paramount.
evidence: Statement about the utility of the methodology with citation to Pienaar et al., 2017

claim: Female New Zealand White rabbits weighing 2.2 to 2.6 kg were used in the study.
source: Female New Zealand White (NZW) rabbits (Millbrook Farm, Concord, MA), weighing 2.2 to 2.6 kg, were maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions and fed water and chow ad libitum.
evidence: Description of experimental animals

claim: The rabbits were infected with M. tuberculosis HN878 using a nose-only aerosol exposure system.
source: The rabbits were infected with M. tuberculosis HN878, using a nose-only aerosol exposure system as described (Subbian et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure with citation to Subbian et al., 2011

claim: At defined time points from 16 to 20 weeks post-infection, rabbits received a single dose of 100 mg/kg moxifloxacin, 75 mg/kg levofloxacin or 100 mg/kg gatifloxacin by oral gavage.
source: At defined time points from 16 to 20 weeks post-infection, rabbits received a single dose of 100 mg/kg moxifloxacin (Chemieliva Pharmaceuticals, China), 75 mg/kg levofloxacin or 100 mg/kg gatifloxacin (Chem-Impex Intl, IL), formulated in 40% sucrose and PEG400 (90:10) by oral gavage.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: Rabbits were euthanized at 2 to 12 hr post-dose, or between the time of peak plasma concentration and the end of the tissue distribution phase.
source: Rabbits were euthanized at 2 to 12 hr post-dose, or between the time of peak plasma concentration and the end of the tissue distribution phase.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: The lower limits of detection for MALDI MSI were 100 fmol or 750 ng/g for LVX, GTX and MXF.
source: Limits of detection (LOD) were assessed as described previously (Prideaux et al., 2015a). The lower limits of detection were 100 fmol or 750 ng/g for LVX, GTX and MXF.
evidence: Description of analytical method with citation to Prideaux et al., 2015a

claim: The laser step size was set at 50 µm for MALDI MSI which enabled small necrotic areas within lesions to be resolved without overlapping of the laser spot on adjacent acquisitions.
source: The laser step size was set at 50 µm which enabled small necrotic areas within lesions to be resolved without overlapping of the laser spot on adjacent acquisitions.
evidence: Description of analytical method
